quote: Wie ist es, wenn ein Tropfen in eine Flüssigkeit fällt.?
english: What is it like when a drop falls into a liquid?
topic: After a remark on a drop falling into a liquid, Hilbert proposes using Fuchs's independence of substitution coefficients from a parameter to build a general inversion problem, giving automorphic functions of two variables (ternary or binary substitutions), with an elliptic-integral example.

triage.modern_statement: This is a one-line physical aside, not a mathematical problem Hilbert stated. In modern terms it could be read as: what is the hydrodynamics of a liquid drop hitting and entering a body of liquid? That covers the splash or crown, the Worthington jet, air entrainment, and the vortex ring the drop forms as it sinks. Hilbert gives no equations, assumptions or link to the rest of the page (Fuchs's coefficients, the inversion problem, automorphic functions), so there is no precise research question to recover.
triage.answered_by: This was not answered as a Hilbert question, and it is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The physics was already being studied in Hilbert's time: J.J. Thomson and H.F. Newall (Proc. Roy. Soc., 1885) on vortex rings formed by drops falling into liquids, and A.M. Worthington's photographic studies (The Splash of a Drop, 1895; A Study of Splashes, 1908). Fluid dynamicists have kept working on drop impact since then.

evidence.claim: Thomson & Newall (1885) were the first to observe and study how a drop falling into a liquid turns into a vortex ring.
Worthington (1908) was the first to study splash dynamics systematically using photographs.
Worthington published The Splash of a Drop in 1895.
A review of drop impact on liquid surfaces (Oguz/Prosperetti) traces the subject back to Worthington.
Recent research on how vortex rings form and behave when drops splash (Nature Communications, 2015).
A modern review describes drop impact as a long-running research problem in fluid dynamics ever since Worthington.

triage.why: The note is a single informal physics question with no mathematical content and no connection to the page's main topic (automorphic functions). It cannot be tied to a specific problem Hilbert posed, and none of his published problems is about it. The phenomenon it describes, a drop entering a liquid, was already under study in his era (Thomson & Newall 1885; Worthington 1895 and 1908) and is still an active area of fluid-dynamics research. Hilbert may have had one of these studies in mind, but the sources don't show that, so it would be speculation.
